records.summary: 430 Beach St is in the C-2 (Community Business) zoning district within the Waterfront 2 Special Use District and the Priority Equity Geographies SUD on the Fisherman's Wharf tourist corridor. The site has operated as a limited restaurant and tea shop since at least 2018, with three health department referrals approved between 2018-01-29 and 2018-04-17. The immediate area is saturated with food businesses: 20 registered food or drink establishments and 11 active ABC on-sale licenses within 500 ft (27 licenses within 1,000 ft), triggering the undue-concentration flag. Mobile food facilities are not covered by the Planning Code rule table, so the pathway analysis shows no use control was looked up and no change-of-use determination was made. The base rate shows zero dated use decisions for comparable businesses within 1,000 ft in the last 10 years (193 records were excluded as building work or agency referrals, and 30 were grant-only permits/licenses), so no approval rate can be calculated.

approvals.summary: The rules could not decide whether a mobile food facility is permitted, conditional, or prohibited in C-2 because the rule table does not cover mobile vending, and the records do not show what 430 Beach St was last used as.

findings.text: The rule table covers bars, restaurants, cafes and nighttime entertainment but has no use control on file for mobile food facilities, so no zoning lookup was performed.

430 Beach St operated as a limited restaurant and tea shop between January and April 2018, with three Planning health referrals approved (filed 2018-01-29, 2018-03-16, 2018-04-12) stating continuation of existing permitted restaurant use in C-2.

The C-2 district has no hours-of-operation control on file (Planning Code § 210.1, in force since before 2022-01-01), so evening or late service would not trigger a conditional use hearing for hours alone.

The Waterfront 2 Special Use District (Planning Code § 240.2) overlays this parcel and may impose additional use, design, or operational controls beyond base C-2 zoning, but the rules as they stood on 2022-04-14 are not exposed in this report.

From 2021-12-20 to 2024-12-20 a change of use or demolition of a laundromat required conditional use authorization under Planning Code § 202.12, but the rules do not know what the space at 430 Beach St was last used as, so this protection does not apply or block the concept.

approvals.summary: A mobile food facility needs a Department of Public Health mobile food facility health permit, which is issued after plan check and vehicle inspection without a hearing and is allowed.

findings.text: A food truck or cart needs a Mobile Food Facility health permit from DPH, covering plan review of the vehicle, a commissary agreement, and the permit application with initial inspection; the 2026–27 annual license fee for mobile food facilities is $0, and the permit application is $470 with plan review of $414 (low-risk) or $690 (high-risk).

The truck must be permitted by San Francisco DPH even if it holds a health permit from another California county; submit two sets of scaled drawings, interior and exterior photos, a menu, and a commissary agreement through the DPH portal.

A certified food protection manager (one per facility, valid 5 years) is required within 60 days of opening; every employee who handles food must obtain a California Food Handler Card within 30 days of hire.

The DPH mobile food health permit application is sent to the Planning Department for zoning review as an interagency referral, meaning Planning will confirm the mobile food use is permitted before DPH issues the health permit.

approvals.summary: The rules could not decide whether a building permit or change-of-use review is needed because a mobile food facility operates in a vehicle or cart, not inside the building at 430 Beach St, and the existing occupancy group of the space is not in the records.

findings.text: A food truck operates in the public right-of-way or on a private lot and does not alter the interior occupancy or use of the building at 430 Beach St, so a building permit and change-of-use review for the fixed structure is not applicable unless the operator installs fixed equipment or makes tenant improvements inside the building.

The existing occupancy group of the space at 430 Beach St is not in public records; only plans or an inspection show it, so whether the building itself would undergo a change of occupancy is not established.

If the truck uses a commissary for food prep and storage, as the concept profile states, no cooking or storage facilities are installed at 430 Beach St and no building permit for kitchen build-out is needed at this address.

expected_conditions.condition: The mobile food facility health permit requires a commissary agreement with a DPH-permitted commissary for food prep, storage, and vehicle cleaning.
expected_conditions.basis: Every San Francisco mobile food permit requires a commissary (catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_health_permit notes commissary agreement is a prerequisite). No nearby mobile food decisions are in the data, but the DPH portal instructions mandate it for all trucks.

expected_conditions.condition: The Public Works location permit will require posting a yellow notice at the proposed site for 10 days, mailing notice to all addresses within 75 feet, and a 30-day public comment period; unresolved objections go to a public hearing.
expected_conditions.basis: The location permit process (catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit) requires on-site posting, 75-foot neighbor notification, and a 30-day comment period, with a hearing if objections are not resolved. The catalog notes location permits are routinely appealed by nearby restaurants.

expected_conditions.condition: The location permit will require $2 million commercial general liability insurance naming the City and County of San Francisco as additional insured.
expected_conditions.basis: The catalog entry for the Public Works location permit states final issuance requires $2M liability insurance naming the City, along with the DPH health permit, fire certificate, and DMV registration.

expected_conditions.condition: Each street location needs a separate Public Works location permit; multiple locations each need their own 10-day posting, 75-foot notification, and 30-day comment period.
expected_conditions.basis: The catalog entry for sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit states Public Works issues a permit for each street location, starting at $1,151 per location. The stall-risk note says to apply for 2–3 candidate locations at once because location permits are routinely appealed.

expected_conditions.condition: If the truck operates on a private lot instead of the public right-of-way, a Planning zoning review and DPH approval are required instead of the Public Works location permit process.
expected_conditions.basis: The catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit states that private lots go through Planning and DPH instead of Public Works. No mobile food precedent on private lots is in the records, but the catalog lays out the alternate path.

expected_conditions.condition: The business must subscribe to organics (green bin) collection service under SB 1383 and may need to participate in edible food recovery above size thresholds.
expected_conditions.basis: California SB 1383 requires every commercial food generator to subscribe to organics collection; cities enforce it through business license or health inspection (catalog entry ca.calrecycle_organics_sb1383). Set up hauler service before opening.

filing_playbook.action: Request a written Letter of Determination from San Francisco Planning Department confirming whether a mobile food facility is permitted in C-2/Waterfront 2.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: State that the concept is a mobile food truck with limited cooking and no alcohol service, intended to operate in the public right-of-way or on a private lot at or near 430 Beach St in the C-2/Waterfront 2 zoning district. Ask whether mobile vending is a permitted use or requires conditional use authorization or is prohibited under Planning Code §§ 210.1 and 240.2, and whether the Waterfront 2 SUD imposes additional restrictions. Provide a one-page concept description and photos of the vehicle if available. Do not file any location permit or sign a commissary lease until Planning confirms in writing that the use is allowed.

filing_playbook.action: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain an EIN from the IRS.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online through bizfile. File the Statement of Information within 90 days ($20 LLC, $25 corporation). Apply for the EIN online at IRS.gov the same day the entity is formed; the EIN is issued immediately Monday–Friday. The entity name and EIN are required for the business registration, seller's permit, bank account, and all city permits.

filing_playbook.action: Register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector and obtain a Business Account Number (BAN), and file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the County Clerk if the doing-business-as name differs from the legal entity name.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register online at sftreasurer.org within 30 days of starting business; the fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55 up to $100k for 2026–27). The BAN is required for every other city permit. File the FBN statement with the County Clerk in person or by mail, then publish once a week for four weeks in a court-approved newspaper and file proof of publication within 45 days. The bank and DPH will ask for the filed FBN statement.

filing_playbook.action: Obtain a California Seller's Permit from CDTFA and register as an employer with EDD if hiring employees.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register online at cdtfa.ca.gov for the seller's permit (free, usually issued the same day); it is required for selling food and drinks. If hiring employees, register with EDD e-Services for Business within 15 days of paying more than $100 in wages; free, takes 1–7 days. Set up workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund before the first employee starts.

filing_playbook.action: Have at least one owner or manager obtain a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate and set up California Food Handler Card training for all employees.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register and take an ANSI-accredited food safety exam (ServSafe, Prometric, 360training, etc.) within 60 days of opening; valid 5 years; cost about $100–$250. Every employee who handles food must complete a Food Handler Card course ($7–$15 online, about 2 hours) within 30 days of hire; valid 3 years. DPH asks for the manager certificate at the pre-opening inspection and the handler card list on file.

filing_playbook.action: Submit the mobile food facility health permit application to San Francisco DPH at least two months before the intended opening date, with vehicle drawings, photos, menu, and a signed commissary agreement.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Apply through the DPH portal with the BAN, two sets of scaled drawings of the truck interior showing equipment and plumbing, exterior and interior photos, a menu describing food prep steps, and a commissary agreement signed by a DPH-permitted commissary. The application is routed to Planning as an interagency referral to confirm zoning approval, then to the Fire Department for vehicle inspection. The 2026–27 fees are $470 application plus $414 (low-risk) or $690 (high-risk) plan review. Schedule the vehicle inspection at least two weeks in advance once plans are approved; the permit is issued after the inspection passes.

filing_playbook.action: Apply for a Public Works mobile food facility location permit for each street location where the truck will operate, starting at least four months before the intended opening date.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File online at sfpublicworks.org for each address; the fee is $1,151+ per location with half due at application. Post a yellow notice at the site for 10 days, mail notice to all addresses within 75 feet, and submit proof of posting. After a 30-day public comment period, Public Works issues a 90-day tentative approval if no objections are filed; unresolved objections go to a public hearing. Final issuance requires the DPH mobile health permit, SFFD fire certificate, DMV registration, and $2M liability insurance naming the City. The catalog warns location permits are routinely appealed by nearby restaurants, so apply for 2–3 candidate locations at once. If operating on a private lot, go through Planning and DPH for a zoning review instead.

filing_playbook.action: Set up organics recycling service (green bin) with a licensed hauler before opening.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Contact Recology or another licensed hauler to subscribe to organics (food waste) collection service as required under California SB 1383 for all commercial food generators. Cities enforce it through the business license or health inspection. Arrange service before the first day of operation.

timeline_cost.notes: The day range (90–270 days) is the time to obtain the mobile food facility health permit and one Public Works location permit when both are granted, not a time to a denial or withdrawal. The health permit takes 30–90 days (catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_health_permit); the location permit takes 60–180 days including posting, neighbor notification, the 30-day comment period, and final issuance (catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit). These run sequentially because the location permit requires the health permit as a prerequisite, so the total is 90–270 days. The cost range ($2,600–$8,500) covers government fees only: entity formation ($70–$150, catalog ca.sos_entity_registration), business registration ($55–$700, sf.business_registration), FBN filing ($60–$120, sf.fictitious_business_name), food safety manager cert ($100–$250, ca.food_safety_manager_cert), mobile health permit ($880–$1,500, sf.mobile_food_facility_health_permit), and one location permit ($1,151–$5,000, sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit). Each additional location adds $1,151–$5,000 and 60–180 days. These figures assume Planning confirms mobile food vending is permitted in C-2/Waterfront 2; if it is not, or if the concept must be changed to fit within a permitted use, no cost or timeline can be given until the zoning answer is known. The stall risk is high: the catalog warns location permits are routinely appealed by nearby restaurants, and the Fisherman's Wharf tourist corridor has 20 registered food businesses and 11 ABC licenses within 500 ft, so neighbor opposition and appeals are likely to push timelines to the upper end or beyond.
